said the decline in long-term Treasury yields supported the sector during the month. Government bonds rallied as investors moved toward safer assets amid a selloff in AI and technology stocks, with the 10-year Treasury yield falling 29 basis points to around 5%. Lower yields generally benefit utilities, which are often viewed as bond proxies because of their stable cash flows and dividend payouts.

Gerard also highlighted a clear divide in the sector's performance: all five of the top gainers were regulated electric utilities or water companies, while the three decliners were merchant power or AI-linked names.

Top utility sector detractors of October

was the sector's biggest decliner, falling 1.84% during the month. Gerard attributed the weakness partly to a broader selloff in AI-linked power stocks. On October 14, NRG fell 5.9% alongside Vistra and Constellation Energy as concerns about CoreWeave's debt raised questions about the sustainability of AI-related power demand and spending.

Gerard noted that the stock was generally higher during the month, supported by strength across nuclear power names following Constellation Energy's Google agreement. However, Vistra fell alongside NRG and Constellation on October 14 amid concerns about CoreWeave's debt. Meta's earnings later revived concerns about AI spending, particularly given Vistra's 20-year nuclear power purchase agreement with Meta.

Gerard described AES as a deal-pinned stock, with its performance largely tied to developments surrounding its planned $15-per-share acquisition by a consortium led by Global Infrastructure Partners and EQT, rather than broader market developments.
